projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John McDonnell was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I was living on -- at [address redacted].

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: In '41? I was 17.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you still in school at that point?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes, I do. I was -- I was driving my father's car and I had the radio on and I think I was out in __+ or some place like that and when I heard the news, I couldn't believe it. But I thought to myself, "where's Pearl Harbor?" I had no idea where Pearl Harbor was at that time. I thought I knew my geography pretty well, but that -- I was stumped on that. And, of course later on when I found out what happened I was -- I was in such shock. I couldn't believe it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So in the months or -- in the months leading up to that, did you have any idea that we would be getting into the war? From what you could --

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, of course right after that FDR made that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mhmm.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: -- speech to the Congress that stated war existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire. And then a few days later as I learned that Germany declared war on us. Which a lot of people were -- I think mistaken that they felt we declared war on Germany but it was the other way around. Germany declared war on us because they were an ally of our -- in with Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any temptation when that happened -- any temptation to run out and sign up?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Oh God, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still in high school at that point?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had another six months to go in high school?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything for the war effort in that last part of high school?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, yeah, we did a lot. I think we did some collection of -- I guess it was the -- what would you call it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Scrap drives? That sort of thing?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, that sort of thing -- we were, you know we were -- but as we got more and more into it we became more and more patriotic, you might say. And of course it had its drawbacks because it was rationing at the time and my father was very stingy with the car because of gasoline and all the rest of the stuff but -- but he was still pretty generous about it but very kind of frugal about it __.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you get the word from Uncle Sam?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, I was out of school and I was just -- I had an older brother that was eight years older than myself. And he -- long before the start of the war, that a lot of his friends were drafted for that one -- one year -- to serve one year and they would be out but he joined them and about -- he was in there about ten months I guess, and when the war broke out, so he was in for the duration, he was in over five years. And like I say he was much older than myself. And he kept writing back to me. "Don't be a fool. Wait. It's going to be a long war and don't jump in and don't try to be a hero. Wait your turn." And I took his advice. Thank God, I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then, so when did you get your draft notice?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: In the -- in the June of '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '43. So in that year in between you worked?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes, well, I was just out of school and then worked. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right, so you got the word from Uncle Sam in June. When did you report?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Right away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You had to report right away.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah. And luckily I went with a lot of good friends in the Lakewood area. And we went to -- we went together down to Columbus, down at Fort Hayes, in Columbus for a few days and then we were all shipped to El Paso, Texas. Fort Bliss, Texas. Actually it was in -- in the -- in the aircraft artillery, 40 millimeters and one thing I was very thankful for, that I wasn't thrown in the infantry. So I bounced around in the -- in the aircraft. We went on maneuvers in Texas and New Mexico and then in -- into California and the Mojave Desert and then to Camp Hahn and after awhile then when the -- the Americans were ready to make the invasion -- we were thrown in the infantry. And so the honeymoon was over you might say. But we went to -- took our infantry training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that first day of infantry training?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, it wasn't as bad as I thought it was because actually we were pretty tough, too. But not -- but it was a lot like an -- we went to Camp Carson, Colorado. Beautiful camp up in -- outside of Colorado Springs. And so we were taking our basic infantry training there. And when the -- when that was over we just kind of waited around and didn't know what -- what our future was going to be. And then all of a sudden we were shipped out and we were going to go overseas. And we went to Camp Kilmer, I think it was in Maryland and then to -- on a ship, one of those lousy, what do you call them, troop ships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that part of a convoy?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes, it was part of a convoy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about that crossing?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: It was -- we were down in the hole and as I remember we were -- we slept in hammocks, about five deep. And as I remember I was number three, right in the middle. And the guy above me was awfully overweight and his big ass came down and I could hardly move -- roll over. And I remember the latrines were so bad. It had salt water that came through and it's -- as it flushed you just, you know, sat on it -- on that god-awful john and you just did your business -- got the hell out of there as soon as you could. And we got just fed once because of the -- of the number of troops. We just got fed twice a day. Seemed like we were always in line either for breakfast and then for dinner but lights out at nine we couldn't --. And it didn't bother me so much because I never smoked and I'm glad I never did. And so then we -- we got as far as Scotland, we landed in Scotland and as soon as we did why we were hustled onto a troop train and went all the way down through northern England down to the southern part of England, outside of London. And there we were in the staging area and no passes or anything we couldn't even get out; we were in. So after -- after that, why the -- this was probably a couple weeks after D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's when you arrived?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, and thank God I missed that. And, so then we went on a -- out of South Hampton, we got on a troop ship, an English troop ship it was a lousy, dirty, rotten ship and got over to France. Went down the rope ladder, down to the LCI, got on that and came into Omaha Beach and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of shape was Omaha Beach in when when you got there?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Omaha Beach was -- you could tell that there was a lot of destroyed equipment, Half-tracks, tanks, other kind of stuff that was strewn around -- equipment. But it was pretty well cleaned up in a certain way. And one of the things I do remember, we were like -- we had -- they made us carry such heavy packs. It was so -- hard, I mean it was just a struggle to carry the -- I don't know how much they weighed but they were just -- and then we -- we went up the side of the cliff and when we got there, why we were met with two-and-a-half-ton trucks. And then they took us to a staging area again and with that all I remember is that my best friend that I had Glen Powell, we were just real close friends all through the -- the service. He was from Lakewood and he went to Lakewood High School but I went to St. Ignatius but he went -- but we were real, real, you know, real close friends. Greatest guy. And then they split us up and I remember saying good-bye to him. And, we said that what we were going -- what we were going to do when the war was over and we just hugged and shook hands. And I remember the first thing I asked my mother when I got home, "How was Glen?" And she hesitate awhile, then she told that the Germans killed him. And to this day I think of him so many times because he was -- I felt so sorry for him because he was the only child and I did meet his mother. His father was dead. And he was so good to his mother, he used to write to his mother all the time and he called me Mac and he said in his letters, "Mac, and I did this and Mac, and I --." And he was always after me to write my mother. I didn't like writing letters. I had another, a younger brother that came in almost a year later when I wrote to him. I said, "For God's sake go -- don't be dumb like your brother. If you -- if you're called up, join the Navy," which he did. And thank God he -- so then we were split up and he went to one outfit and I went to another. I was sent to the 79th Infantry Division, Company C, 315th Regiment, know it well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go over as replacements then?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I went over as a replacement. Actually, --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you with your buddy before you guys got split up?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Oh, just a week or so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just a week or so?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah. Our division landed D-Plus Six. Of course I missed that. And we had a record of the greatest number of days on the front line and in fact I was captured on the 24th of October. On the 23rd, the 313th and the 314th Regiment were off the line and we were to go off the next day. And so I didn't go off -- I went off the line, but not -- I went off the line with the Germans. Not with the -- not to R and R.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else do you remember about the campaign in France before you were captured?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, it was like a typical infantry. We just dug foxholes and sweated out barrages. I remember -- I remember so much of rain that it seemed like it was raining all the time and we'd have to bail out the foxholes and remember we were always told if we could to put covers over our foxholes because of -- of the tree burst that killed so many and that's -- that saves you. We always worked as a buddy system. And if one was doing something one -- and I remember this one time we made -- we made an advancement and we got -- it was so pitch dark that we got our -- he was told to go back and bring up supplies. Well, and I was told I was on guard duty. And he thought I was digging the hole and I thought he was digging the hole and by the time he got back and I was off guard duty we were so damn tired we just didn't figure on it. But we paid for it the next morning because all the other guys were dug in. And as we got up, we were so close to the Germans they were just spraying us with small arm fire and boy we just hit that dirt and start digging. And another time I remember -- was made another attack and I got out in front with this great guy, this sergeant. And we just kept going and going and God it was -- we were full of sweat and we got to a point where we just stopped and -- and he -- he was a smoker and he asked for cigarettes and I said, "yeah, I got them." I mean I liked candy and he -- so we traded. I traded him a pack of cigarettes for a chocolate candy bar and he kept saying, "We're all right, Mac, we're going to make it, we're going to make it." And all of a sudden we heard these shells coming in. It was -- we could tell the incoming mail and outcoming mail, which was which. It was our own artillery coming in. It was either the observer got it and the coordinates mixed or we didn't or maybe we went too far. I don't know. But it was one of the worst barrages I ever went through and it was our own. And he went one way and I went the other. He was killed. And it just, you know, just like that. And then leading up to my capture was that -- we were -- we were fighting in this -- wooded hilly area and I was -- I was the first scout and we had already taken this little French village. It had little farm -- farmhouses in it. And -- and as I was leading the platoon we came outside of this little village. We had cover -- the road was up on a -- up on a -- like a hill, and we were down in a ravine which -- and we had tree cover and we got outside of that village maybe a mile or so and came to an area of about ten yards, it was open area. And I double-timed across. And my second scout he came and them Germans must have had it zeroed in, because they -- they hit -- hit a mortar 88 shell right between the two of us and all I could remember is flying in the air and coming down. And I reached down and __+ on my side and the handle was blown off and I reached down and I felt my leg and "God, I'm hit." In a way, I kind of was -- I always -- when guys got hit, they were sent back. We call them, "You lucky son of a bitch, you're going sleep in a -- in between sheets tonight," you know. But it -- it wasn't much, but this poor guy behind me, he got it really pretty bad. And up on the road this battle was going on and on and a TD, a tank destroyer, came along and he was picking up walking wounded. And he called down to -- and so I told him, you know, I was hit and he said, "Well, come on up." So I got up there and I just -- my buddy, I said I'd be back for him, and he said, "Come, please do." He was pretty well hit. So I got on that tank destroyer and went into that little village that we just left and by this time they had built a -- an aid station and they were bringing in all the wounded in there and I'll never forget that scene. That was a bad scene. Guys who, they were all screaming and crying and doctors trying to tell these guys they're going to live and -- and then ones that didn't make it there was a -- like a fence or a road -- beside the road where they just would take the dead bodies and drop them off behind the road but -- so -- I held -- I saw that they had stretchers on a Jeep and I hailed him, and I told him about -- that about my buddy and he said, "Do you know where he is?" and I said, "Yeah, I do." He said, "Okay, hop in." So we went down to that place and sure enough there was -- he and another one were there. So we got both of them out. We put them on stretchers and we took them back. And then -- I had -- my pants -- I lost my rifle, I lost my pants and underwear were all gone I had to get new -- and so I went to -- I, you know, supply sergeant or whatever got -- then I got word that these guys up on the front where I should have been were taking such a hell of a beating and they were asking for anybody come back up with ammunition and K-rations, anything I could carry. So I loaded myself up with bandoliers and hand grenades and stuffed my shirt with K-rations and stuff like that and -- and I came up and the sergeant greeted me, he said, "What are you doing here?" I said, "Well, you want?" And he said, "Oh, for God's --." Well, luckily for me, we had just taken over this German kill box and he said, "You get in there." And because the next day we were going to go off the line and he said -- and God, I got in there and there was straw on the floor and there was a lot of German equipment around and logs in the top and I felt pretty safe, you know. But all night long they -- of course the Germans knew exactly where, they had it zeroed in, hitting all around. And they were hitting so close to where other guys who were out in the open. Three more came busting in the place. And one was a sergeant. I was only a PFC. The other one was a sergeant. I didn't even -- he was from another squad. And we waited and waited until the barrage was over. That was during the night, and then early in the morning I heard these rumbling of tanks. I said to the sarge, "We got to get out of here. Those are German tanks." He said, "They are like hell! Those are our tanks!" I said, "Sarge, those are German tanks, I know they are." "No, they're not." So we waited. And sure enough he could tell, he said, "God, you're right." So he says, "Just stay down. Maybe they'll pass by. We don't know we were in there." Well, there was four, Mark IV Tiger tanks and the lead tank -- right over -- came over -- right over our passageway, and I went over with him and when I was looking out, I saw this German, I was ready to shoot him and just then a voice came out, our CO, he was first lieutenant, he hollered to us, "Come on out, you guys, they know you're in there." So he said to the sarge, "What do you want to do?" He said, "throw down your --" so we went out. And luckily this German, had a potato masher in his hand. Five seconds later he would have thrown that thing in and it would have killed all five of us, but then they dispersed us. And we were on the German side and -- and that was another scene. Got over there -- the CP and actually the German soldiers were pretty good to us I mean they were -- they weren't like us, I mean we were terrible when we took prisoners. These guys were kind, in a way, I thought. And it was just getting light, I heard this -- we used Piper Cubs as artillery observers and I thought, Jesus Christ, I hope this guy doesn't spot us because all there was around us was all this German equipment, Half-tracks and trucks and everything else. And sure enough he spotted us, and I went through the worst damn barrage I ever went through in my life. And I went -- we all just, you know, you didn't care if you were German or American or what you were and I went for a hole and this other guy came right next to me. I covered up and I looked over -- it was a young German soldier, we were eyeball to eyeball, sweated out that barrage and after that was over they took us back and we marched, I don't know how many couple days till we got to Strasbourg and that was a staging area that they brought all, you know, prisoners in. But -- from different areas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in France when your were captured then?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in France when you were captured?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you know the -- close to any town or anything?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yes, it was close to -- just outside of Lunaville.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mhmm.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Which is south of Nancy, I think, yeah. And we had a hell of a lot -- a lot of battles right there and it was -- I -- after, after the war I got this -- the 79th Infantry Division, the combat book, about -- and it goes -- like day-to-day battles and everything of where it was and I looked up that date and we were -- it was quite -- they describe it as -- as a -- the Panzer Group and the SS Groups that we were -- we were fighting and they were one of the topnotch -- and it was -- so we put up a hell of a battle but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that was in October, right?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: That was in October, yeah. October 24th, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: October 24th. So what happened after you were taken to Strasbourg then?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, we -- we waited around there for a while and then they loaded us on trucks and sent us -- I would -- I almost could say that it was in the Black Forest because it -- I went back to Germany after the war and I know -- and it was in an area __+ you know beautiful country but -- and we came into this little town and it was like a -- they had a sawmill and a few homes and church and school and stuff like that. And I remember there was two truckloads of us guys. I don't know how many we were. And all these little kids came running out and cheering and I said, "Get out of my face you little krouts!" you know. And they were so -- you know here we were defeated army and so they housed us in this schoolhouse. Took the -- everything out and just threw straw on the floor and that's where we were and our job was to clean out -- working this -- in the forest with these German foresters or whatever they would call it. And it was kind of open and we were still in our combat gear, you know, except we didn't have the cartridge belt of course, and everything else but we had the steel helmet and we used the steel helmet as our bowl for our soup, you know. We took, the -- course we wore the liner and had this -- and we used that. And one funny thing happened, I -- they asked for volunteers and which I don't usually volunteer but it was to peel potatoes for the -- for the Germans and so I -- I was peeling the potatoes and I had my -- my steel helmet there with -- kept the peelings. And so I snuck those back in and I hid them and this German officer came back and he's looking for the guy that was peeling the potatoes, he wanted those peelings for his horse and of course the guys -- they didn't, you know, let on so -- but I -- I we had a little stove in there, you know, cold stove. I used to put pieces of potatoes on the like -- try to make a like French fries or something -- ate those. But, oh, then this other fellow and I, we kept talking about you know, we could probably get out of here, we could probably escape. But, so one night I was real -- the six guys that take off we didn't know who they were or anything about them and the German soldier, the guards came roused us all. It was a cold November night, raining and everything and -- God, they came around and were whacking us and everything else, asking us who we -- who they were and where they were going and this that and the other thing. And of course we didn't know, but they kept us out there for hours. And so with that, the thought of trying to escape would -- because I figured if we did, the other guys would suffer and one of the first things you're taught when you're -- don't try to be a hero for God's sake because you're going to make it miserable for the rest of them -- and so they shipped us out took us to Stuttgart, as I remember, and put us in like I remember a horse farm, barn. God, did it stink. It was -- and it was cold and miserable. And when I was -- when I was -- the day I was captured when I was on the German side, I got hit in the back of the leg. It went right through my leggings and it didn't bother me too much and -- but then later on after I took -- I got -- was all discolored. And so I showed it to this German guard and he sent me to this little clinic, little civilian hospital, you might say. They were real good, real good to me. They took the shrapnel out. And I got to stay there a couple days. I didn't want to leave, it was so nice. But, oh, and then while I was there they captured these six guys. And they put them in like a pen and -- 6 x 6 x 6 or something like that. All these guys could do is just run around trying to keep warm. And, but then, then they put us on boxcars and it was a couple of days on the boxcars and I got dysentery so bad I remember on that boxcar. And, oh Jesus, what a bad scene that was. So finally we got to Stalag VII-

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: And first thing I remember is they took all our clothes. And they issued us new clothes. With a -- they gave us a big bowl and a spoon and an overcoat and one pair of thin socks and we were sent to this area, south lager at Stalag VII-A where the newcomers come. And I remember this Sergeant Major of a British Army comes in and he was an old-timer. He was a prisoner that was -- British soldier that was taken at Dunkirk and he was giving us advice. "Don't be a hero. This war is going to be over soon. And you're only going to make it worse for everybody else if you do try to escape. So just hand it out." And he says, he's kind of an oddball, he says, "See these boots?" They were beautiful. "I shine these boots everyday." He had such a _ and so -- so I got sick a couple of times with dysentery and it was so bad that one time I -- I was so sick I thought I was going to die. Then I was afraid I was going to live because I was so miserable. But I got through it and kept going on work details and they put us on boxcars and take us into Munich and mostly the work we would do would be on railroads or we would be cleaning up the streets or the buildings for the bombing -- the British bombed at night, the Americans bombed at day. And when -- when the siren would go, the alarm would go off, the guards would haul us into air raid shelters right with the civilians. And we'd go down there, the Americans were bombing and we were down there with children and they were screaming and crying and, God, we were there for the longest time. Then we'd, after the all clear signal came out, we'd have to go out and start all over again. And a couple of times, Dachau was northwest of us, Stalag VII-A was northeast of us but the same -- but a lot of times they -- they would send those political prisoners down on work details like we were. And I remember that winter, the '44 and '45 was one of the coldest, that -- I see a lot of these poor Jewish -- they had the Star of David on their -- looked like striped pajamas they were wearing rags and wooden covers on their feet. God, their faces looked like skulls and I thought, my God. We had it bad, but nothing like those poor devils. I felt so sorry for them. I never realized what -- till later after the war what really happened to these people. But I knew it was bad. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you went on these work details were they --did you volunteer for those or did they make you go on those?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: They made you go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mhmm.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: But, in one way, it was a blessing in disguise; you got an extra ration of food. You got your soup at noontime. And while -- while they would set it aside till -- when you got back maybe 10 or 11 o'clock at night by the time you got back. But then we get a ration of food while you were -- while you were in -- in Munich which was -- which was good in a way. Another thing that was good, we did a lot of trading. We -- first thing we learned to do is to sew a big -- in the back of our army coats -- we sewed big pockets. And for some reason or other the guards would search us all but they never seemed to search there and we got Red Cross parcels every once in awhile, not all the time but not -- but once in a while we would get them and they would divide it up, you know. We were six on a cart and we'd count the raisins, and count the cubes of sugar, and the cigarettes, and luckily I didn't smoke. I'm glad I didn't, because smoke -- cigarettes were worth their weight in gold. The Germans loved our cigarettes and a lot of times when we'd go in -- even the civilians would come up and would want to trade bread for it -- and for five -- for five cigarettes I could get a kilo of bread and that was great we kept that price. We'd get five kilos. Five cigarettes for a kilo. That's it. And then we made other -- other details I was on -- and one time I got some eggs and another time it was -- but potatoes I remember working in a de -- next to a farm where we had to sift through and we'd sneak off to these -- they'd bury their potatoes --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before you were captured what was your job with the -- with your outfit? Were you -- did you say you were a lead scout?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, I was first scout.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: First scout, okay.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, I -- then I acted as squad leader -- assistant squad leader and I was up for promotion, which I didn't get, but that's all right. In a way, sergeants -- you know the Germans had a funny way about rank. If you were a noncom, even a sergeant, you couldn't work. And I found out later one of the reasons why all the Air Force guys, no matter what their job was, they were automatically a sergeant so that when they were captured Goreen(ph) had a deal about the -- he honored the Air Force, even the enemy Air Force that -- so they never went to work, I mean, I never realized that till later but I remember like in that movie Stalag 17, or whatever it was, they were all sergeants, they didn't work. And -- but they made us work and -- but in a way we could -- we could pick up stuff and there was debris all the time. We had to bring back stuff for -- we made our own stoves and we bought that wooden and we brought back old kettles and pots and pans and stuff like that anything, we were like real scavengers, you know, and so in a way it was better than sitting around in the -- although it was, you know, it's trading one thing for another, which is worse. And, but sometimes it was really bitter cold and I remember several times when we would be -- you never knew when that train was going to pick us -- cold -- and you'd be waiting and you don't know how many, how long you're gonna be and just to get inside of it -- 20 degrees warmer maybe, but at least -- but, but we lived through it. And -- all I can remember is that I was lucky in a lot of ways. I wouldn't go through it again for a million dollars, yet I wouldn't take a million dollars to say I never went through it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Stalag VII-A was in Moosburg, is that right?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: 7A -- yeah. Moosburg, mhmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you there the whole time?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, most of the time. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mhmm.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: And then -- and then Pat came crashing through and he gave us a real nice talk. He was -- I don't know if you ever saw that movie Patton but George C. Scott played his part. He looked just like him, I mean, God, they could have been doubles. But, I remember him giving us a real patriotic talk or speech or something and he was so proud of us and all that sort of stuff. Made me feel good. I mean, it -- you know you had mixed feelings about -- God, you were captured, you know, you weren't -- I wasn't ashamed of it, but what was I going to do? -- I was either -- if I didn't do what I was supposed to, I would have been dead and four other guys would have been killed, too. I mean so, sometimes I look at it that way. And, but I don't know which hell was worse -- worse, the fighting and the combat for six months or the six months or seven months as a prisoner of war. So there was two different hells.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to keep up on war news much when you were in the camp?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Not too much. The only bad news we got was during the Bulge when the -- they were -- they were like pushing it -- the Allies back to the Atlantic Ocean and then we -- then we got a lot of guys that were pouring in as prisoners and telling us how -- how rough it was and what they went through and so it -- but it was short-lived and sometime after that why then we -- we -- we felt pretty good about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about life in the camp?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, we -- we had this one guy that I really admired. I don't know he must have been a schoolteacher or something. He could speak about four different lang -- five different languages and he -- he was something like that Bill Holden in that movie, he had all kinds of equipment and stuff and he had a way about him and -- and he was also a very religious -- I'm a Catholic and he -- there was four barracks in our compound and every night about 11:00 o'clock or so he'd walk through each one of them say -- I say the rosary at such and such, you know, at a certain time, ten minutes from now or -- if you want, fine, you could go or you didn't have to or wanted to -- and I remember going to it several times. And what a great guy he was. And he just -- he'd always end it with, "We're going to say a special prayer for the guys -- for the guys that were killed today." And it was something that -- it was just -- I wish I could have kept in touch with him because to me he was just a -- a wonderful person. God love him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able --

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: But he --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: But he -- nobody razzed him. Or said any, you know -- they knew he was brilliant. They couldn't he -- knew that if they made any fun of him they couldn't do it and but he was just such a guy that was so con -- convincing and -- and just a loving guy that you just had to admire.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to do much to pass the time -- to amuse yourselves in any way?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Ha, not too much. Only try to get rid of the lice and stuff like that. I got two letters while I was there, one from my dad and one from a girl that I hardly knew. She lived next door to a girl that I was dating. And I was kind of thrilled to be getting that because she was so, God, I remember she was such a good-looking gal. And why -- and she -- she was going to junior college at the time in Massachusetts. And why that letter got through I don't know. Sexy Susie Shmock(ph). I'll never forget. (Laughs). I still have that letter. And I've been looking trying to find her but she moved away and I don't know -- I lost track of her. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long was it before your family found out that you were a prisoner?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I guess -- my folks got a telegram on November the 7th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay, two -- two weeks?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or was that the MIA telegram or --?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, missing in action.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let me read it there for the microphone, "The Secretary," this is dated -- let's see where's the date on this?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: November --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: November 7th, 1944. "The Secretary of War desires me to express his deep regret that your son, Private First Class John R. McDonnell has been reported missing in action since 24th October in France and further details or other information are received you will be promptly notified. Signed the Adjutant General," I can't quite make out his name, "J. A. Ulio," is that right?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And so then how long did they -- before they finally got the word that you had been taken prisoner?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I think it was some time in January.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mhmm.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I know it was after Christmas bec -- and I'm not -- I'm not certain when -- when that was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any parcels or -- when you were in there -- Red Cross parcels?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I never got any - well, I got Red Cross parcels but not, I mean, not individual.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: They were always divided up among six of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you talked about the earlier about -- how we were a little bit meaner to the prisoners we had taken. Did you witness any of that? Of us being mean to the German prisoners?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, a little. I tried to keep -- stay away from it because some guys were mean and maybe justifiably -- but I knew that they were -- I knew that they were -- they were like us. And I remember so many of the guards that -- they would talk to us about -- "We didn't want to be here either." And, "Why are we fighting?" And I remember so often when I'd get on that -- boxcars and especially in, when in the spring when they opened the doors and going back and look out on the fields in Germany and I said, God, what a beautiful country. Why are we -- why are we -- why, why? It was crazy. And they were -- a lot of them were the same way that we were. But then there was a lot of mean bastards, too. But, most of the guards I would say were probably older men that were too old to -- or they were a lot of them were like cripples that were shot up in the -- on the Russian Front probably or something like that and they couldn't -- they weren't able to go back and so this was limited service for them to be a guard. But, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After you were liberated by Patton, what happened next?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, we -- they had -- according to Geneva or whatever the rules of war -- that your prisoner of war camp cannot be bombarded or -- for 48 hours. So we felt they -- we want you to stay here and be safe. But they came in and they deloused us as best they could and they brought us some food and -- but actually it was a lot longer than that and because they were moving so fast at that time. This was April the 29th when we were liberated but it was like May the 7th or 8th when we were finally -- we got out of there. It was -- we were put on transport, I think they were C-54, and were flown to Camp Lucky Strike outside of Cherbourg and waited there for a while and then shipped home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were there any celebrations in the camp when V-E Day came along? When you were -- that -- it sounds like it happened when you were still in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Not too much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not? Just relief.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I mean we were just -- we were still, weak.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: And, but we were lucky that, you know as soon as we got back to Camp Lucky Strike we got -- first thing they did was take our uniforms off and - just, I mean they were just full of lice and everything. It was -- gave us good showers and new clothing and good food and all that sort of stuff. And I saw a movie I remember seeing the first movie was the Good Earth. __++. And, just waited around until we -- we were going to be shipped home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And when did you get back to the States?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When? I mean, I don't mean exactly.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: I don't know the date --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- roughly how long were you at Camp Lucky Strike -- maybe a month or so?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mhmm.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Yeah, sometime in June.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sometime --

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Latter part of June, I guess. Then I was home for 63 days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got --

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Terrible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Well, what a disappointment that was. Well, first of all my two brothers were in the service and they were away. All my friends were gone. My mother, God love her, had a nervous breakdown. And that was a bad scene and the girl I was with -- she dumped me. (Laughs.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sorry I asked.

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: And all I did was get drunk and drink a lot which was - (chuckles). But, so it was not a, you know -- sometimes I would see these movies about every -- how wonderful it is to come home. Well, it didn't happen to me. No parades, no nothing. I didn't give a shit, but at least I would have had something but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind about your time in World War II?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: Not that I just -- have a -- I love this country and I would have died for it. But I hated the Vietnam War and I hate this Iraqi War. I think it's madness and I just hope that this Bush gets beat. I think it's just crazy. And what it's going -- I feel so sorry for the troops, the poor guys that are over there. When I look at them and I see them carrying that stuff around, at least we knew who our enemy was in that, but these guys in that sweat and that swamp over there and my heart just goes out to them -- I think, God, if - if Cheney and Bush, and the rest of them, went one week where I went through they sure as hell would have found a way to not rush into that crazy war. We had no right. But, I have -- I have a time convincing some of the people that I know about that but I don't give a damn what they think. I know how I feel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: John McDonnell
sp.p: That about covers it.
